items.title: How job hunting became an expensive cash suck
items.summary:
There’s an expense that’s easy to overlook when talking about the cost of living : getting and keeping a job. 

We tend to think of work as the thing that pays the bills, but commuting and the other costs associated with it come with a price tag of their own. In a recent TikTok video posted in October, content creator Char shared that she had just had to quit her job because she could no longer afford the commute. 

Char, who lives in the UK, said the amount of money she used to spend on a full tank of fuel now only filled her car halfway. And with fuel prices showing no sign of easing, she said, the commute was only going to get more expensive.

“I can’t afford to keep driving to work,” Char said. “I can’t afford to live. Something has to give.” 

And right now, she decided, that something was her job. She would have to search for a position closer to home. 

In the comments, people shared they had been in a similar position recently, also highlighting how everything else had hit them financially, such as grocery prices and rent.

Commuting costs are also affecting people looking for work. Some job seekers have shared online how the expense of traveling to interviews is becoming difficult to manage. One creator said in a recent TikTok that she can no longer afford the job hunt.

“Assuming you get past the 12,000 rounds of phone screens and Zooms, and you are invited to an on-site interview, what if you don’t have the money to commute?” she said.

Compound that with the fact many are interviewing at several different companies at once, she said, and the costs quickly rack…
items.t: How job hunting became an expensive cash suck

items.title: Why employees are ‘habit hugging’ at work
items.summary:
If you’re prone to hanging on to the way things always used to be done at work, you might be “habit hugging.” It’s where employees hold on to familiar routines even after new tools and processes have been introduced.

Habit hugging may be a sign of insecurity, or a form of self-preservation — finding stability and control in a working world that feels increasingly unfamiliar.

A new report by online learning platform TalentLMS , based on a survey of 1,500 US employees who had received training on a new tool, technology, process, or way of working in the previous 12 months, found that 65% of respondents said letting go of an old habit is harder than learning a new one. And only 41% consistently used a new way of working after they were trained on it. Meanwhile, 42% admitted they still used tools or processes their managers believed had been replaced.

Multiple industries are evolving and being disrupted by AI . Habit hugging could be a response to the pressure employees feel to continually adapt as everything changes around them. As uncertainty grows both inside and outside the office, sticking to what you know may offer a little comfort.

There’s a tension between employers demanding adaptability and employees being expected to maintain productivity throughout that change: The report found that 48% of respondents felt rushed to adopt new ways of working. Employers aren’t necessarily helping their workforce overcome their old habits when they expect them to adopt new systems without slowing down or making mistakes.

That pressure may also make employees reluctant to admit…
items.t: Why employees are ‘habit hugging’ at work

items.title: Can potential clients find you using AI?
items.summary:
A few months ago, I got a DM on LinkedIn from someone wanting to interview me for a feature she was writing. At the end of the interview, I asked her how she found me. She replied, “ChatGPT.” 

If you’re running a solo business, you’ve probably thought about how people find you online. Maybe you even track the information by asking or through a “How did you find me?” question on your website.

Many people now ask an AI chatbot for a recommendation, the same way they’ve typed questions into Google for years. No matter how you feel about using AI tools personally, AI search is something that may have more and more of an impact on your business over time.

AI as the new recommendation engine 

For a long time, getting found online meant search engine optimization (SEO), or showing up in Google results by publishing content like a blog. The newer version is AEO (answer engine optimization) or GEO (generative engine optimization). The idea is that AI tools might “find” you the way Google once did.

AEO and SEO share the same fundamentals. AI tools pull from publicly available information on the Internet, so the more you put out there, the easier you are to find. 

In BrightLocal’s 2026 Local Consumer Review Survey , 45% of consumers said they used ChatGPT or another AI tool to get recommendations for local businesses. A year earlier, it was 6%. That’s a big jump in a single year. The survey looked at local businesses, so it may not line up exactly with the work you do, but directionally it suggests that more and more people are turning to AI search to find what they’re looking…
items.t: Can potential clients find you using AI?

items.title: Some people don’t use AI at work—and feel judged for it
items.summary:
New workplace fear unlocked—and it’s not being yelled at for heated-up fish in the office microwave or getting too merry at the Christmas party. 

As companies continue to invest billions in their AI strategies, nearly half of employees fear judgment for not using artificial intelligence enough at work. 

That’s according to the third annual Inclusion Initiative report from London School of Economics (LSE) and consulting firm Protiviti, which surveyed 3,001 professional employees between March and May 2026. With AI spending forecast to grow to $2.59 trillion this year—up 47% from 2025—the AI transition is no longer a personal choice, but is transforming workplace norms and expectations. 

When AI first entered workplaces, more workers feared judgment or being caught out for using the technology. Now the opposite is true: 48% worry about being judged for not using AI enough, compared with 20% who worry about being judged for using it. 

Almost three quarters of those surveyed (74%) now use AI at work, up from 29% in 2024. But the pressure to adopt AI in workflows has birthed a new kind of busywork—workers are pretending to use AI even when they aren’t. 

A separate report by software firm Visier found nearly half of workers (48%) said they have “ exaggerated their AI usage or expertise to colleagues or leadership ” to keep up with expectations.

While organizations understand the importance of equipping their workforces with AI tools, there is still work to be done when it comes to supporting employees with AI adoption. 

Only 39% of users have built AI into a standardized…
items.t: Some people don’t use AI at work—and feel judged for it

items.title: Screen time got your brain fried? Try a ‘brain stack’
items.summary:
Every few months, like clockwork, a new analog trend emerges in an effort to get us all off our phones. . .and of course, document the process for social media. 

The latest is “brain stacking”: keeping a stack of puzzle books, novels, non-fiction and other phone-free activities in a neat pile within arm’s reach, in lieu of doomscrolling. 

Online, thousands of people have proudly shared their “ stacks ”. One popular creator, Mandy Rulez, regularly shares timelapse videos of her brain stacks before work , starting her morning with nearby stacks of non-digital activities, like journaling, before moving on to a sudoku, a crossword, and finally a quick ten pages of reading. 

Other creators are also incorporating timers into the mix . For example, a 12-minute brain dump in a spiral notebook, followed by ten minutes of planning, 15 minutes of puzzles, 20 minutes of coloring. Total brain stack: one hour. 

Brain stacking is a continuation of the “ analog bag” trend earlier this year (otherwise known as, well, simply “doing things.”) But we’re in an era when “ brain rot ” and “doomscrolling” have become part of our everyday lexicon, so it’s easy to see the appeal. Gen Z, after all, are the ones embracing dumb phones and buying up Bricks in an effort to reduce their screen time.

The idea of “habit stacking” has existed in the world of self-help for years, and involves stacking new habits to existing ones. More recently, bedtime stacking , as well as peptide stacking , have emerged as online trends. Then there’s goal stacking and income stacking . Clearly, queuing up back-to-back…
items.t: Screen time got your brain fried? Try a ‘brain stack’

items.title: Workers hoard AI knowledge to stay competitive, Anthropic report says
items.summary:
AI tools are becoming increasingly ubiquitous, but the best techniques for using them are likely still a secret.

This is because workers who develop highly effective AI tricks have no incentive to share them with their colleagues or their bosses, notes a report published Monday by Anthropic.

Researchers interviewed 66 executives, managers, and employees at 58 of Anthropic’s corporate customers and found that many workers are reluctant to share their best AI tricks, citing reasons ranging from job security to more leisure time.

The practice has frustrated managers looking to exploit AI-driven efficiencies. The report quotes one exasperated executive saying, “They don’t want you to know, because they want to use those 10 hours a week to go walk their dog.”

AI hoarding is a new form of the age-old workplace phenomenon of knowledge hiding, in which employees deliberately withhold information from their coworkers to retain a competitive edge. 

Employees in the AI age have even more at stake: their jobs. If the trick they develop is powerful enough, they might render themselves redundant. And even for those whose jobs are secure, revealing a time-saving trick might just mean they are assigned more work.

That raises a thorny question for business leaders: How do you incentivize employees to help automate their own jobs?

Employers hoping to discourage AI hoarding may need to rethink how they measure and reward productivity . Otherwise, employees might realize that their most valuable professional asset is something they’re better off keeping secret.
items.t: Workers hoard AI knowledge to stay competitive, Anthropic report says

items.title: 6 tips to use this Thanksgiving when family asks about your career
items.summary:
Evan Reece has a few strategies for handling unwelcome questions about his career when he gathers with family. He founded and ran a ski lift ticket platform for 15 years, but it went out of business during the COVID-19 pandemic . Reece then started a career management platform. He’s its sole employee and earns less than he did before.

At family parties, he sometimes feels pressure to explain why he doesn’t get a full-time job working for someone else. When he’s asked such questions, he reminds himself that people usually ask because they care.

“Oftentimes, if we’re stressed about something that we don’t have an answer to, the question feels like an interrogation, when that’s rarely the intention of the person asking the question,” said Reece, 48, who runs the career management platform Truest.me.

A simple “How’s your job going?” can feel like an ambush when you’re unemployed , underemployed or working in jobs your friends and relatives don’t understand or may regard as frivolous. These queries can bring up painful experiences like layoffs . Advice can sound like criticism to recent graduates in a seemingly impenetrable job market , while curiosity about someone’s income can feel like judgment.

Even inquiries motivated by a genuine desire to connect can come across as invasive or awkward in a group setting.

With holiday gatherings approaching , here are some tips and potential scripts to help you handle tricky career conversations with relatives and feel less defensive. The same strategies can be applied when faced with scrutiny about getting married or having…
items.t: 6 tips to use this Thanksgiving when family asks about your career

items.title: AI can help moms. It can’t replace the village
items.summary:
Susan (pseudonym) regularly goes to AI for parenting help. When her child is sick, she checks whether she needs to call the doctor. When her toddler is acting out, she looks to AI to find out if it’s normal. But then, she takes the question to her online parenting group at Peanut to double-check.

She already has an answer. So what is she still looking for?

AI is always there. When we have a question at 2 a.m. and no one else is awake, we can ask Claude. When we fear judgment, ChatGPT will almost always validate. Is AI going to replace the “parenting village” we were all supposed to find?

Maybe, but probably not.

Curious about how this is all playing out, I went looking for answers in a few places. I started with Michele Battersby, president of Peanut, an online community platform for mothers. Her team looked at public conversations on the platform mentioning AI over 90 days. Mothers were asking about everything: health, development, sleep, feeding, and all the life logistics that go with parenting.

But while they were asking these questions, it seems AI was often just a starting place. AI can give us information. It can be a place to ask a question that we might otherwise feel embarrassment about. It can even help with the mental load (more on that later). But even with all of that, mothers on the app were still going to other mothers for support and to talk about their actual experiences.

Because sometimes we’re looking for more than an answer.

I’ve been thinking about this as AI becomes part of what we’re calling the parenting village. I recently asked my LinkedIn…
items.t: AI can help moms. It can’t replace the village

items.title: Americans are sick of disruptive leaders, data shows
items.summary:
Business culture has long lionized bold, disruptive leaders. But these days, at least, Americans are yearning for some stability. 

In a survey conducted shortly after the midterm elections, 82% of Americans said they prefer leaders who “get things back to normal rather than shake things up” and 82% also said they prefer a “stable and predictable” life.

The New York-based global public relations firm Burson interviewed about 1,600 Americans across party lines. The poll was published November 14.

An overwhelming 90% of respondents also said they want honest, calm, consistent leadership, and 75% said they lose respect for CEOs who change positions under pressure.

It is easy to interpret these findings as a reflection of current public opinion about President Donald Trump. Trump’s penchant for disruption and his brash businessman image helped him win the White House twice, but the outcome of the midterms—and the results of the Burson survey—indicate that the public has grown tired of the chaos.

In a separate Associated Press poll, about two-thirds of the roughly 100,000 midterm voters surveyed thought Trump has the wrong priorities, while 7 in 10 said Congress hasn’t been doing enough to check the president’s power.

As Fast Company reported earlier this month , the midterm results also illustrate the risks organizations face when they become overly dependent on a single charismatic leader. Successful leaders can make subordinates increasingly reluctant to question their judgment, even when circumstances change.

“At some point, you have to ask whether people are…
items.t: Americans are sick of disruptive leaders, data shows

items.title: How Nvidia employees feel about Jensen Huang’s return
items.summary:
The public reaction to Jensen Huang’s return has been mixed at best, raising the hackles of lawmakers and corporate governance experts. Even the stock price took a bit of a dip after surging by over 30% on Monday. Within the company, however, the mood appears to be considerably lighter. 

In videos that are circulating across social media, Huang received a hero’s welcome at Nvidia headquarters, where his employees lined the walls cheering for him. Between chants of “Jensen! Jensen!” and “We love you, Jensen,” he addressed his staff in a display of contrition. 

“I’m terribly sorry for putting all of you through all of this,” he said. “I’ve made some very terrible mistakes, and I’m going to work on coming back.” After an employee threw her arms around Huang in a tight hug —lasting over 10 seconds—he continued: “Thank you all for the second chance. I’m going to be a better CEO the second time around.”

Many Nvidia employees have taken to LinkedIn to express their relief over Huang’s return, seemingly overlooking the indiscretions that led to his ousting. They heaped praise on their newly reinstated CEO, describing him as the “ heartbeat of Nvidia ” and “ one of a kind .” 

One employee even invoked Charles Dickens , paraphrasing the opening of A Tale of Two Cities : “It was the worst of times, it is the best of times. It was the season of Darkness, it is the season of Light. It was the winter of despair, it is the spring of hope. We had nothing before us, we have everything before us.”

Another employee claimed he always knew Huang would return to Nvidia: “When Jensen…
items.t: How Nvidia employees feel about Jensen Huang’s return

items.title: Why your boss can basically fire you for anything—and why it’s not like that outside the U.S.
items.summary:
We’ve all seen the scene play out in media: A character stands up at work, dramatically declares they quit, and walks out of the office for the last time. While many people will surely empathize with that desire, the reason why a sudden resignation is possible in the U.S. isn’t as great as such a display makes it out to be. 

Mostly because it goes both ways: an employer can axe you at the drop of a hat, in theory—even without a warning, PIP, or other chance to improve.

The U.S. has something called at-will employment , which means that you can leave—or lose—your job without giving any notice.

A job that’s at-will “can end at any moment, for good reason, bad reason, or no reason at all, and with no procedural mandates,” says Gali Racabi, an assistant professor at Cornell’s School of Industrial and Labor Relations and an associated faculty member of Cornell Law School. 

Currently, at-will employment is the law of the land in Washington, D.C., and every U.S. state except Montana. 

“This makes work in the US really easy to sever,” Racabi says.

He adds: “The at-will rule is a travesty, and a mark of moral flaw in our economic order. We need to do away with it ASAP.” 

Critiques of at-will employment 

Despite being the default in America—a country whose culture is associated with entrepreneurialism, independence and one that favors employers without much safety-net protection for workers—at-will employment causes a number of concerns. 

Most prominent, perhaps, is a person suddenly losing their income and the many repercussions that can come with that. The practice is…
items.t: Why your boss can basically fire you for anything—and why it’s not like that outside the U.S.

items.title: Why your HSA needs a succession plan
items.summary:
Health savings accounts are usually discussed in the context of their trifecta of tax benefits: pretax money going in, tax-free compounding while the funds are inside the account, and tax-free withdrawals for qualified healthcare expenditures.

But HSAs have their limits. The HSA’s tax benefits effectively cease upon the account owner’s death, or the death of his or her spouse if that person is the beneficiary.

That makes it crucial to have a succession plan for your HSA: a plan to encourage tax-free spending during your lifetime (and your spouse’s, if you have one), as well as naming the correct beneficiary for the account to maximize the tax benefits.

HSAs give during your lifetime . . . 

Whereas tax-sheltered retirement account owners will pay taxes on the dollars they put into a retirement account (Roth) or on their withdrawals (traditional tax-deferred), HSAs are a unicorn account type—the funds are tax-free every step of the way, provided you spend the money on qualified healthcare expenses.

Those tax benefits are magnified for people who pay their healthcare expenses out of pocket, invest in long-term investment assets, and are in higher tax brackets.

Given those prodigious tax benefits, an HSA investor would have a bigger balance than a person investing in an IRA, 401(k), or taxable brokerage account, assuming the same contribution amounts, rates of return, tax rates, and holding periods. That’s because investors in those other account types pay taxes along the way: at time of contribution (Roth), during accumulation (taxable), and/or at time of withdrawal…
items.t: Why your HSA needs a succession plan

items.title: AI upended entry-level jobs. Here’s what employers are actually looking for
items.summary:
AI is changing nearly every aspect of the workplace—but especially entry-level jobs, to the point where Gen Z is calling for millennials (who are only in their 30s and 40s) to retire to make room . Many are placing the blame on AI for making tasks in many entry-level jobs outdated; data seems to back that up.

A recent survey of nearly 7,000 workers, managers, and executives found that 51% believe AI is reducing early-career opportunities, while 49% say tasks that traditionally helped employees build work experience are increasingly being handled by AI. Another shows that entry-level listings have plummeted 35% since 2023; another suggests entry-level jobs in New York City have been cut in half .

That means the pressure is on for early-career candidates to show employers what they can bring to a role beyond their ability to use AI tools. A catch-22 emerges: many employers increasingly turn to AI, yet many also want candidates who can think independently, come up with original ideas, recognize when to put the technology aside and trust their own judgment.

Indeed, many young workers find themselves in a tricky-to-navigate, even unfair entry-level job market. Luckily, there are tips that can make you stand out in a labor market that both increasingly relies on AI, and that also demands workers show employers the human skills they’re looking for.

items.title: Who gets to decide what ‘bad things’ we should accept about AI?
items.summary:
There has been intense debate about the threat AI poses to humanity and what should be done about it. The voices have piled on: a former Anthropic researcher who said AI companies are “ gambling with our lives ,” prominent tech executives including Anthropic’s Dario Amodei calling for an AI slowdown , politicians refusing to back down from the AI arms race with China , and investors dismissing it all as hysteria standing in the way of “ the largest wealth-creation event of our lifetimes .” 

Then, Sam Altman said out loud what they’ve all been dancing around : “We believe the world should accept some bad things happening for the benefits of this technology.” 

Altman isn’t alone in this belief. The AI industry as a whole wants the world to trust that the benefits will be worth the “bad things” that happen, even as companies pursue trillion-dollar valuations despite their own warnings. Those decisions are being shaped largely by a small, powerful group of men. 

Our research shows the problem goes well beyond a few CEOs. Over the past several months, our team at the Shorenstein Center at Harvard Kennedy School studied how AI is used, experienced, and understood by men and women in the U.S. We found that women are underrepresented across many of the critical places where AI is developed, adopted, and discussed.

Start with coverage. In our analysis of more than 78,000 news articles about AI over the past year, men were named in AI headlines 14.6 times as often as women and cited as experts 4.3 times as often. Part of that reflects who leads AI companies, but the gap still…
items.t: Who gets to decide what ‘bad things’ we should accept about AI?

items.title: Will AI take your job? 3 principles for making yourself harder to replace
items.summary:
The Navier-Stokes equations , first formulated in the early 19th century, are widely used today to help design airplanes, create computer graphics, and even predict the weather. Yet for almost two centuries, a central question about them remained unsolved. We knew the equations worked in practice, but no one had proven whether they always hold up mathematically without breaking down.

That all changed in September when OpenAI claimed to have solved the Navier-Stokes problem, followed on October 6 by a torrent of proposed breakthroughs across nearly 400 math problems that had baffled researchers for generations. As Cornell University mathematician Steven Strogatz explained in an Atlantic essay , the announcements have left the field reeling. How should people think about their work when a machine can do it so much better?

Strogatz is no ordinary mathematician. A pioneer in the field of nonlinear systems and network science, he is also an award-winning author and a sometime New York Times columnist. His livelihood is not in danger. Yet OpenAI has him asking, “What’s the point?” It’s a question we’re all going to have to answer. Here are three principles that will help you figure it out. 

Principle 1: The Infinite Monkey Theorem 

The Argentine writer Jorge Luis Borges had a fascination with a concept known as the infinite monkey theorem . The idea is that if you had an infinite number of monkeys pecking away at an infinite number of typewriters, they would randomly create the collected works of Tolstoy and every other masterwork ever written (or that could be written).…
items.t: Will AI take your job? 3 principles for making yourself harder to replace

items.title: Women’s AI leadership is bigger than the data shows
items.summary:
Every study on women in AI seems to say the same thing. Women are disproportionately impacted yet are hugely underrepresented in AI roles, not making the decisions that have such an impact on the world. The latest comes from LinkedIn, whose recent research found that women accounted for just 26% of U.S. AI hires in 2025 , against 50% of hires into non-AI occupations. Across 27 countries, women hold only 13% of C-suite AI leadership roles at AI companies. Thus, they make up a ridiculously small percentage of the best-paid jobs in the economy. 

That’s very worrying. The people designing these tools and running these companies decide what the technology is for, whose tasks get automated, and how the value is captured. If women are left out at every stage, the products and the profits will reflect it. The gender gap will get bigger because of that. 

But after reading some of these studies, I’ve started to wonder if they don’t also have a few blind spots of their own. In denouncing women’s absence from AI, we may fall into the old habit of downplaying what women actually already contribute because it happens in places we don’t count and fail to see.

I interviewed Sarah Steinberg, who leads global public policy partnerships at LinkedIn, at the Reykjavík Global Forum this week. Steinberg told me LinkedIn’s research on AI leadership shows women are more likely to hold jobs exposed to AI and less likely to have AI skills. 

But do the numbers fully capture women’s AI contribution? She agreed we may be underestimating women in AI leadership. And we had just been in a session in…
items.t: Women’s AI leadership is bigger than the data shows

items.title: Does culture change people’s personalities?
items.summary:
Personality is often misunderstood. For instance, people tend to think they are way more unpredictable and complex than they are according to others, to the point of mistakenly assuming that their “personality changes from one situation to the next”. In fact, everybody has a preferred pattern of reactions to different situations, and if you hang out with people long enough you will have no trouble predicting how they are likely to act in any given situation, or indeed understanding what makes them tick.

And yet, even if humans are predictable , that doesn’t mean that they are rigid or unable to flex according to the demands of the situation. One of the earliest findings in psychology is that behavior is always a function of both the person and the situation, which means that in order to predict how people will act you must take into account not just who they are but also what the situational requirements are.

Micro vs. Macro 

At the micro -level, this explains why personality may be “suppressed” or inhibited in strong situations, that is contexts where there is a great deal of pressure to behave in a specific way or form: from a church (quiet, respectful, pensative) to a nightclub (loud, extraverted, energetic), to a lecture (focused, pensative, attentive), to a soccer game (depending on where you are, anywhere from excited and energized to aggressive and stressed). That is not to say that people stop being who they are when they are required to inhibit their personality; but rather, that personality becomes a weaker predictor of behavior when the strength of the…
items.t: Does culture change people’s personalities?

items.title: The conversation you’re avoiding is already costing you
items.summary:
It’s 2 a.m., and a capable leader is wide awake. In their mind, they’re replaying a difficult conversation that hasn’t happened yet. They’ve been waiting for the “perfect time”: a calmer week, a better mood, the right moment. The irony is that they can approve a major budget without blinking, yet they’ve spent the last few weeks avoiding a five-minute talk. And it’s not because they don’t care. It’s because they care a great deal about the person, the relationship, and the work.

The organizational psychologist Liane Davey makes a useful distinction here. Conflict aversion is the natural discomfort most of us feel when a conversation could go badly; conflict avoidance is what happens when we let that discomfort drive our behavior. Avoiding a difficult conversation may buy some relief in the short term but it usually costs far more later on. 

But something else is going on when leaders avoid difficult conversations. By staying silent, they’re deciding for the other person that they can’t handle it, don’t want to know, or will react badly.

What employees actually want 

Employees do want to know. In a March 2024 survey of 1,500 employees in Canada and the U.S. by the Achievers Workforce Institute, two-thirds said they want to have tough conversations at work. But one-third said they don’t feel safe having them with their manager, and fewer than one-third say they trust their managers .

That gap is the real story. People aren’t asking to be protected from hard truths. They’re asking for two things: the truth, and a safe way to hear it.

Let’s agree that not every…
items.t: The conversation you’re avoiding is already costing you

items.title: The midterm elections revealed an AI backlash. Here’s what it means for CEOs
items.summary:
Hello and welcome to Modern CEO ! I’m Stephanie Mehta, CEO and chief content officer of Mansueto Ventures. Each week this newsletter explores inclusive approaches to leadership drawn from conversations with executives and entrepreneurs, and from the pages of  Inc.  and  Fast Company . If you received this newsletter from a friend, you can  sign up to get it yourself  every Monday morning. 

I was in Silicon Valley for part of last week, where many investors, founders, and executives seem to shrug off the midterm elections, in which voter distrust of big tech and AI safety played a role in the blue wave. Their conclusion? Data centers—those massive, resource-heavy computing facilities—simply have a “PR problem.” They maintain that the tech sector needs to launch a charm offensive to remind communities of all the good that will come from these massive computing facilities, such as jobs and support for small businesses. Heck, the tech giants might even send some employees to volunteer at local schools! 

A growing concern 

This interpretation of the election results is naively narrow and largely misses the point. “Data centers are the foil,” says Jim O’Leary, CEO of the global advisory firm Penta. “They’re the face of the AI backlash, but the issue is bigger.”

Indeed, a Pew Research Center report published in August found that 52% of Americans said they are more concerned than excited about the use of artificial intelligence in daily life, up from 37% in 2021. items.title: Need to solve a problem? Neuroscience says try the Jack Reacher Method
items.summary:
There’s a point in Lee Child’s book Make Me (the 20th in his Jack Reacher series , for those keeping score) where Reacher is trying to solve a problem and decides to back-burner it: Instead of actively working the problem , he sets it aside, trusting his subconscious to eventually make the right connections.

Which it does.

Sound kinda hokey?

Actually, no. Neuroscience shows you tend to be at your most creative when you’re not trying to be creative. Actually, you’re at your most creative when you’re not trying to do anything at all.

Researchers at Washington University in St. Louis used PET scans to determine which parts of the brain lit up during different types of activity . To establish baselines, some participants were put in the scanner and told to do nothing, what the researchers called “resting state.” Surprisingly, resting state resulted in mental energy spikes across various brain regions.

In fact, mental energy turned out to be higher in resting state than active state, where participants were given mental tasks.

A few years later, neuroscientist Nancy Andreasen made resting-state activity (she called it “free floating periods of thought”) her focus. No tasks. No inputs. No intentional creativity. No nothing; just vegging. 

As Andreasen writes in The Creating Brain: The Neuroscience of Genius :

Most investigators made the convenient assumption that the brain would be blank or neutral during “rest.” From introspection I knew that my own brain is often at its most active when I stretch out on a bed or sofa and close my eyes.

We found activations in multiple…

items.title: A truism for our political leaders: until work again involves respect and decent levels of pay, this crisis will continue | John Harris
items.summary:
Last week’s Milburn review contained telling phrases, but the core problem is not Neets: it’s what capitalism as we know it has done to employment

Everyday pride and contentment. That’s what work should give us. In 15-plus years of speaking to ordinary people and politicians about the UK’s serial woes and crises, one thing has revealed itself to me time and time again: the mess of cant, contradictions and tensions in our national understanding of work. Indeed, the higher up the hierarchies of power and influence any conversation about work goes, the more one vitally important subject seems to fall away: what paid employment actually is or ought to be.

All of this is reflective of a very British kind of amnesia. Of course poorly rewarded, unreliable jobs have always been part of our economy – and in the past a focus of fierce social conflict. But well within living memory a combination of the power of trade unions and the collective social conscience built into the postwar consensus resulted in an economy and labour market that now seem almost inconceivable. For sure they were scattered with restrictive practices and base prejudice: fathers securing jobs for their sons, people from minorities being excluded from work not just by people in management but by their fellow workers, and a great deal of…
